catalog_citation: Edwards, Owen. 2012. Grammatical functions in Tolaki. BA (Honours) thesis, School of Language Studies, The Australian National University. 109 pp. hdl:1885/9388 (open access, ANU Open Research; pdfTeX).
catalog_locator: p.48, sec. 5.4.1.1 'Nominative Prefixes', paragraph introducing examples (46)-(48); saved file (109 pp., pdfTeX, author Owen Edwards)
catalog_quote: Although these indexers have been called prefixes, in certain environments they do not occur prefixed to the verb. When the verb occurs after the conjunctions ke ‘if/when’ or a ‘and/so’, or if the sentence is negated using oki, the prefix is attracted forwards and is suffixed onto the conjunction forming a phonological word with it, as defined by stress placement. This is illustrated in examples (46)-(48) below, in which the prefix has been attracted forwards, altering the stress pattern of the previous word as well as the verb. Stress in Tolaki falls on the penultimate syllable of a word. Secondary stress is then assigned from right to left to every second syllable. Primary stress in the examples below is indicated with an acute accent and secondary stress with a grave accent. (46) a. * No-máte masína, a kù-petúha to-óna. ... b. No-máte masína, á-ku petúha to-óna. ... The engine died so (then) I got out. (47) a. * Ke ù-mbúle ì-kambó-mu, iámo kolùpe-'áku. ... b. Ké-u mbúle ì-kambó-mu, iámo kolùpe-'áku. ... When you return to your village don’t forget me. (48) a. * Óki nò-kií-'i inóno o-mánu. ... b. Okí-no kií-'i inóno o-mánu. ... He didn’t see this chicken.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word; secondary stresses on every second syllable leftward from the primary (alternating trochaic pattern from the right edge). The domain is the phonological word including attached clitic prefixes, so stress shifts when a nominative prefix attaches to a preceding conjunction or negator (e.g. No-máte masína, á-ku petúha; Ké-u mbúle; Okí-no kií-'i). Corroborated family-wide by Mead 1998:16 ('Stress is penultimate (non-phonemic), with suffixation usually precipitating stress movement') and 1998:97.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'Secondary stress is then assigned from right to left to every second syllable' (marked with grave accents in exx. 46-48, e.g. kù-petúha, ì-kambó-mu, kolùpe-'áku).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Stress is computed over the phonological word: prefixes attracted onto ke-/a-/oki carry or shift stress (ex. 46-48). Mead 1998:16 adds for the family that suffixation moves stress (i.e. stress is computed on the suffixed word) and that phonetically long vowels are vowel sequences (Mead & Tambunan 1993:5-6 on Tolaki).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (root plus affixes/clitics), running-text examples rather than citation forms; Edwards' data are from the Konawe (Kendari/Wawotobi) area with Mekongga speakers also consulted.
new_statements.identity_note: Edwards 2012 describes Tolaki proper (tola1247), data mainly from the Konawe dialect (Kendari/Wawotobi/Hopa-hopa) with Mekongga speakers also consulted; he notes the two main dialects differ lexically. Mead 1998's statements are for all Bungku-Tolaki languages including Tolaki. The Mekongga volume (Mahmud et al. 1995) describes the western Tolaki dialect and is silent on stress. No Glottolog dialect codes assigned here.
